oliveira.name: Church of Our Lady of Oliveira
oliveira.short: A Gothic collegiate church on the site of Mumadona’s monastery of 949, with the Padrão do Salado in front
oliveira.long: Countess Mumadona Dias founded a monastery here around 949, and in the 12th century it became the rich Collegiate of Santa Maria. After his victory at Aljubarrota, King John I kept a vow and rebuilt the church in Gothic style in 1387–1413; the Manueline tower was added around 1513. In the square in front stands the Gothic canopy of the Padrão do Salado, raised in memory of the battle of 1340, and beside it grows an olive tree, the symbol of the miracle of 1342 that gave the church its name.
oliveira.history:
It began with a monastery. Around 949 Countess Mumadona Dias founded a house on the low ground of Vimaranes, dedicated to the Saviour, the Virgin and the Apostles; at first it was a double monastery for monks and nuns. In 1074–1075 Pope Gregory VII banned double monasteries, and by 1089 it was a house for men only. Around 1139 it became the Collegiate of Santa Maria de Guimarães, one of the richest church institutions in late-medieval Portugal. Of the 12th-century Romanesque church there remain one wing of the cloister, the front of the chapter house and a capital from the main portal.

In the 14th century the collegiate became a centre of pilgrimage to the image of Saint Mary. On the eve of the Battle of Aljubarrota in 1385 King John I made a vow to her, and in 1387 he paid for the rebuilding of the church. The design is attributed to the court architect João Garcia de Toledo. The main work was finished by 1401 and the last in 1413. Three naves with a projecting transept follow the usual plan of the mendicant orders; the great west window, arranged like an altarpiece with a Tree of Jesse, is one of the finest Gothic compositions in Portugal. Around 1513 a battlemented Manueline tower was raised over the church.

A legend gave the church its name. The Visigothic king Wamba is said to have brought an olive tree from Jerusalem and planted it at São Torcato; in the 14th century it was moved to the main square, where it withered. In 1342 the merchant Pero Esteves set up a cross beside it, said to have come from Normandy, and three days later the olive turned green again. The townspeople saw a miracle, and Our Lady of Victory became Our Lady of the Olive Tree. The cross still stands under the Gothic canopy of the Padrão do Salado, raised by King Afonso IV to mark the victory over the Moors at the Salado in 1340. The olive tree stood in the square until 1870; in 1985, when the square was restored, a new one was planted in its place.

In the 17th and 18th centuries the church was remodelled to the taste of the day: under Pedro II the chancel was deepened and the interior dressed in gilded carving. Twentieth-century restoration uncovered the medieval granite walls and columns again. The collegiate was dissolved in 1911 and re-established in 1967. The former cloister houses the Alberto Sampaio Museum with the collegiate’s treasury. The church has been a National Monument since 1910 and is part of the historic centre inscribed by UNESCO in 2001.
facts: Mumadona Dias founded the monastery around 949.

The dates on the olive tree’s kerb, 1342, 1870 and 1985, mark the tree’s three lives.

oliveira.tip: The church opens Monday to Saturday 8:30–12:00 and 15:30–19:30, Sundays 9:00–13:00 and 17:00–20:00; entry is free. From Largo da Oliveira, the Gothic arcade of the old town hall leads straight into Praça de Santiago. The Alberto Sampaio Museum is in the cloister behind the church; a combined ticket with the castle and the Dukes’ Palace costs €13.
